Can a particle beat light?
Light can be slowed down.
In pure water,
for instance, light travels
at approximately 225,000
kilometers per second,
which is about
three-quarters of its
maximum speed in empty space.
The electromagnetic fields
of the water molecules
interact with the passing
light waves, creating a
cumulative delay that slows
down the wave front.
Now, imagine a high-energy
particle, such as an
electron ejected from a
decaying radioactive fuel
rod, entering that same
pool of water.
That energetic electron
might plunge into the
water traveling at 250,000
kilometers per second.
In that specific
environment, the electron
is moving faster than
the local speed of
light in water.
What happens when a
physical particle outpaces
light within a physical
medium?
The result is one
of the most stunning
sights in nuclear physics,
known as Cherenkov radiation.
When an aircraft travels
faster than the speed
of sound in air,
it creates an acoustic
shock wave, a booming
pressure front that shakes
the ground.
Similarly, when a charged
particle travels faster
than the phase velocity
of light in a
medium, it generates an
optical shock wave.
As the electron speeds
through the water,
it polarizes the surrounding
water molecules, which
quickly snap back to
their resting states,
emitting photons as they
relax.
Because the electron is
moving faster than the
emitted light waves can
travel through the liquid,
those light waves pile
up behind the particle,
forming a coherent,
cone-shaped electromagnetic
shock wave.
To human eyes,
this optical shock wave
radiates as an eerie,
luminous blue glow,
illuminating the deep
cooling pools of nuclear
reactors worldwide.
Cherenkov radiation proves
that the true cosmic
speed limit is not
simply how fast light
happens to be moving
inside a room or
a glass of water.
The true limit is
the invariant constant
c, the speed of
light in the pure
vacuum of space.
The electron in the
nuclear pool did not
break the universal speed
limit of 299,792 kilometers
per second; it merely
overtook light that had
been slowed down by
a crowd of molecules.
